en: [Volume I, Part 1: The Section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa): The Conduct of the Four Castes.
Now, therefore, in ancient times, the sages questioned Vyāsa as he sat with one-pointed concentration on a peak of the snowy mountains in a forest of Devadāru trees. (I.1.1)
O son of Satyavatī, tell us correctly about the Dharma that is beneficial for human beings, as well as the rules of purity and conduct, in this current Kali Yuga.
Having heard those words of the sage, he who was like fire or the sun, possessed of great splendor and learned in the Śruti and Smṛti, replied along with his disciples. (I.1, p. 65) // Par_1.3 //
"I am not an omniscient knower of all truths; how then could I speak the Dharma?
Our father alone should be questioned," Vyāsa said to his son.
Then all those sages, desiring to know the true meaning of dharma, placed the sage Vyāsa at their head and went to Badarikāśrama. (I,1, p. 68) // Par_1.5 //
It was strewn with various flowering creepers, adorned with fruit-bearing trees, endowed with rivers and springs, and graced by sacred bathing places. (I,1,p. 70) // Par_1.6 //
Abounding with the cries of beasts and birds, surrounded by divine shrines,
and adorned with the dances and songs of yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
In that assembly of sages, the son of Śakti, Parāśara, of great splendor, was seated comfortably, surrounded by a host of preeminent munis. (I.1, p. 73) // Par_1.8 //
With palms joined in reverence, Vyāsa, together with the sages,
honored him with circumambulations, salutations, and hymns of praise.
Then, with a heart full of contentment, the great sage Parāśara, that bull among sages, sat down and said, "Welcome; speak. (I.1.75) // Par_1.10 //
Having said, "It is well; you have spoken correctly," Vyāsa immediately asked:
"O you who are kind to your devotees, if you know [the answer], [tell me] out of affection for me or because of my devotion" (I,1, p. 77). [Pariccheda 1.11]
"Tell me the Dharma, O father, for I am worthy of your favor.
I have heard the Dharmas of the Mānavas, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa. (I,1, p. 78) // Par_1.12 //
The Gārgya and Gautama [smṛtis], as well as those remembered by Uśanas, Atri, Viṣṇu, Saṃvarta, Dakṣa, and likewise Aṅgiras; Parāśara 1.13.
And likewise from Śātātapa, Hārīta, and Yājñavalkya;
the laws composed by Āpastamba, as well as those of Śaṅkha and Likhita.
Those composed by Kātyāyana and likewise those of the sage Prācetasa have indeed been heard by me as proclaimed by you; the meanings of the Vedas have not been forgotten. (I,1, p. 79) // Par_1.15 //
In this Manvantara, throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā, all dharmas arise in the Kṛta age and all are lost in the Kali age. (I,1, p. 80) // Par_1.16 //
Tell me something of the common conduct shared by the four castes, which must be performed by those learned in dharma belonging to all four castes. (I,1, p. 87) [Par_1.17]
"Speak at length, O knower of the true nature of Dharma, concerning both the subtle and the gross.
At the conclusion of Vyāsa's words, Parāśara, the foremost of sages, [replied]: (I,1, p. 92) // Par_1.18 //
He has declared the determination of Dharma, both subtle and gross, in detail.
Listen, my son, I shall speak; let the sages likewise listen. (I,1, p. 93) // Par_1.19 //
In every kalpa, through their destruction and rebirth, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are always the determiners of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.

No one is the author of the Veda; rather, having remembered the Veda, the four-faced Brahmā likewise remembers the Dharmas, as does Manu in each successive interval between Kalpas. (I.1, p. 112) // Par_1.21 //

The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different, and those in the Kali age are yet another, according to the nature of each age. (I,1, p. 117) // Par_1.22 //
"In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā, knowledge is said to be so; in the Dvāpara, they say sacrifice alone; and in the Kali age, charity alone. (I,1, p. 119) // Par_1.23 //

In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu are prescribed; in the Tretā, those of Gautama; in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, those of Parāśara are remembered. (I,1, p. 122) // Par_1.24 //
One should abandon the country in the Kṛta age, leave the village in the Tretā age,
the single family in the Dvāpara age, but in the Kali age, one should abandon the doer himself.
In the Kṛta age, one falls merely by conversation; in the Tretā, by touch; in the Dvāpara, by taking food; but in the Kali age, one falls through action alone. (I,1, p. 123) // Par_1.26 //
In the Kṛta age, the curse takes effect immediately; in the Tretā, after ten days;
in the Dvāpara, after one month; but in the Kali age, after a year.
In the Kṛta age, a gift is given after approaching [the recipient]; in the Tretā, it is given after being invited;
in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali, it is given through service.

The highest gift is that given after approaching [the recipient]; the middling is that given by calling out; the lowest is that given to one who has already asked; but a gift through service is fruitless. (I,1, p. 124) // Par_1.29 //
For in the Kali age, dharma is conquered by adharma, and truth by falsehood; kings are defeated by thieves, and men by women.
The Agnihotra sacrifices fall into neglect, reverence for the guru perishes, and maidens give birth [to children]—this is always the case in this Kali Yuga. (I,1, p. 125) Par_1.31 //

In the Kṛta age, however, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā, they depend on the flesh; in the Dvāpara, on the blood; but in the Kali age, they are situated in food and such. (I,1, p. 126) // Par_1.32 //

One should not find fault with the duties that exist in each age, nor with the twice-born who exist in each respective place; for those twice-born ones take their form according to the age. (I,1, p. 128) // Par_1.33 //
In every age, however, the remaining capacity [for penance] has been described by the Sage;
and the expiation declared by Parāśara is also prescribed. (I.1, p. 131) // Par_1.34 //
"Having recollected all of that this very day, I speak it to you; let the preeminent sages hear the conduct of the four castes. (I.1, p. 140) // Par_1.35 //
The doctrine of Parāśara is meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin; it was conceived for the sake of the Brahmins and for the establishment of Dharma. (I.1, p. 141) // Par_1.36 //
The conduct of all four castes is the protector of Dharma;
for those whose bodies have fallen away from conduct, Dharma turns its back. (I,1, p. 143) // Par_1.37 //
Constantly devoted to the six duties, honoring the deities and guests, and eating only the remnants of the oblation, a Brāhmaṇa does not come to ruin. (I,1, p. 145) // Par_1.38 //

Bathing at the twilights, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, worship of the deities and guests, hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice—these are the six duties to be performed day after day. (I,1, p. 218) // Par_1.39 //
Whether he be beloved or hateful, a fool or even a scholar, a guest who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is indeed a bringer of heaven. (I,1, p. 395) Par_1.40.

One should recognize as a guest a person who has arrived from a long journey, who is weary, and who appears during the Vaiśvadeva offering; one who arrives before that time is not a guest. (I,1, p. 396) // Par_1.41 //
One should never treat a resident of one's own village as a guest; because he comes without fixed regularity, he is therefore called a *atithi* (guest). (I.1, p. 398) // Par_1.42 //
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and the like, by offering water for the feet (*arghya*), a seat, and by washing his feet. (I.1, p. 399) [Par. 1.43]
A householder should generate joy in [the guest] by means of faith, the gift of food, pleasant inquiries and replies, and by following after him as he departs. (I,1,p. 400) Par_1.44.
If a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated, the ancestors of that person do not eat for fifteen years. (I,1, p. 401) [Par_1.45]
For him whose guest departs with hopes frustrated, even a thousand loads of wood and a hundred jars of ghee make his burnt offering useless. (I,1, p. 402) // Par_1.46 //
One should sow seed in a good field and deposit wealth with a worthy recipient; for what is sown and given in a good field and to a worthy recipient does not perish. (I,1, p. 403) // Par_1.47 //
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or learning;
rather, one should conceive of the deity within the heart, for he is composed of all the gods. (I.1, p. 404) // Par_1.48 //
For the Brahmin who is steadfast in his vows is unprecedentedly excellent, just as a guest is unprecedentedly excellent;
both of them are ever more distinguished day by day through their constant devotion to the study of the Vedas. (I,1, p. 406) Par_1.49 //

But when the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has commenced and a mendicant has arrived at the house, one should set aside food for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva and then dismiss the mendicant. (I,1, p. 408) // Par_1.50 //
Both the ascetic and the student are the rightful owners of cooked food;
having eaten without first giving food to these two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wandering mendicant should give three portions of alms to the student and the ascetic;
thereafter, if he has the means, he may give as much as desired without restriction. (I,1, p. 409) // Par_1.52 //
One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, then give alms, and again give water;
that alms is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is like the ocean. (Pariccheda 1.53)
He whose parasol, horse, and elephant-rider are magnificent, and who occupies the station of Indra—therefore, one should not challenge him. (I,1, p. 410) // Par_1.54 //
A mendicant is capable of removing the sin committed during the Vaiśvadeva rite;
however, the Vaiśvadeva rite does not remove the faults committed by the mendicant. (I,1, p. 411) // Par_1.55 //
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite—let them all be known as fruitless; they fall into an impure hell. (I,1, p. 412) // Par_1.56 //
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and excluded from hospitality all go to hell and enter the womb of a crow. (Parāśara 1.57)
Whether he be a sinner, a Caṇḍāla, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a killer of his father—
if he arrives during the Vaiśvadeva rite, he is a guest who leads one to heaven.
He who eats with his head wrapped, he who eats facing south, or he who places his hand on his left foot—verily, the Rākṣasas consume that food. (I,1, p. 413) // Par_1.59 //
For that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being neither observant of vows nor learned in the Vedas, the king should punish; for it provides sustenance to thieves. (I.1.60)
For the Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and wielding the rod of punishment,
should conquer the armies of others and protect the earth according to Dharma.
One should pluck flower after flower, but not cut the root;
one should be like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-maker.
The pursuit of wealth, as well as dealing in gems, the protection of cattle, agriculture, and trade—these are declared to be the occupations of a Vaiśya. (I,1, p. 476) // Par_1.63 //
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is declared to be the supreme duty;
if he performs anything otherwise, that shall be fruitless for him. (I.1, p. 480) // Par_1.64 //
Salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—these do not become defiled for those of the Śūdra caste; one may sell them to all classes. (I,1, p. 484) Par_1.65 //

By selling the flesh of animals that may not be eaten, by eating what is forbidden to eat, or by having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his status at that very moment. (I,1, p. 486) Par_1.66 //
By drinking the milk of a brown cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Vedas, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla.
[Volume I, Part 2:

Hereafter, [I shall describe] the ritual conduct of the householder in the Kali age—the common dharma pertaining to the four castes and stages of life according to one's capacity. (I,2,p.1) Par_2.1 //
I shall proclaim that first, according to the words of Parāśara: "A Brahmin, engaged in the six duties, may also perform the work of agriculture. (I.2, p. 3) // Par_2.2 //
One should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted;
a Brahmin should not drive a bull that is deficient in limb, diseased, or impotent. (I,2, p. 6) // Par_2.3 //

One should cause [the bull] to carry for half a day— provided it has firm limbs, is free from disease, is well-fed, bellows pleasantly, and is not a eunuch— and afterwards, one should perform a ritual bath.

A twice-born man should practice the recitation of prayers, the worship of the gods, burnt offerings, and the study of his own Veda; he should feed one, two, three, or four Snātaka Brahmins. (I,2, p. 8) // Par_2.5 //

In a field ploughed by himself, and with grains acquired by his own efforts, he should perform the five sacrifices and cause the initiation for a sacrifice to be carried out. (I,2, p. 9) // Par_2.6 //
Sesame seeds and liquids must not be sold; however, grains and things equal to them may be sold.
For a Brahmin, such means of livelihood as the selling of grass, wood, and the like are permissible.
If a Brāhmaṇa should practice agriculture, he incurs a great fault; the sin that a fisherman incurs in a year, he incurs in a single day. (I,2, p. 13) // Par_2.8 //
With an iron-tipped wooden pole, the plowman, the fisherman with his net, the hunter, and likewise the fowler [each catch their prey] in a single day. (Pariccheda 2.9)
The non-giver and the cultivator alike share equally in the consequences;
for they have cut down trees, broken the earth, and killed worms and insects.

A farmer is liberated from all sins by means of the threshing-floor sacrifice, provided that he does not fail to give to the twice-born when he has arrived at the root of his harvest heap. (I,2, p. 14) // Par_2.11 //
One should designate that thief and that most wicked man as a slayer of a Brahmin;
having given a sixth part to the king and a twenty-first part to the gods. (I,2, p. 15) // Par_2.12 //
By giving a thirtieth part to the Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins;
even a Kṣatriya, having practiced agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra should likewise engage in agriculture, trade, and the arts;
however, those Śūdras who perform improper acts are those who have abandoned service to the twice-born. (I,2, p. 16) // Par_2.14 //
They indeed become short-lived and undoubtedly go to hell;
this is the eternal law for all four castes.
Therefore, I shall now declare the purification for birth and likewise for death: Brāhmaṇas become pure after three days in the case of a death or a birth (sūtaka). (I,2, p. 204) Par_3.1 //
A Kṣatriya is purified in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days,
and a Śūdra is purified in a month, according to the words of Parāśara.
In the case of attending upon Brahmins, purification of the limbs occurs;
however, in the case of the birth of Brahmins, touching the body is prescribed. (I,2, p. 212) // Par_3.3 //
A Brahmin is purified by ten days, a Kṣatriya by twelve days, a Vaiśya by fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified by a month upon birth. (I,2, p. 213) // Par_3.4 //

A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day; one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days; but one who is devoid of both is purified in ten days. (I, 2, p. 215) // Par_3.5 //

A Brahmin who has fallen away from his birth-rites and duties, who neglects the twilight worship, and who is a Brahmin in name only, shall be impure for ten days following a birth. (I,2, p. 217) // Par_3.6 //

But heirs who share a single funeral cake (*ekapiṇḍa*), even if they have separate wives and dwellings, shall undergo that period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for them both at birth and in the event of death. (I,2, p. 219) Par_3.7 //
That impurity (sūtaka) within the lineage ceases with the fourth generation as an heir, or with the fifth born of one's own family. (I,2, p. 221) // Par_3.8 //
In the fourth [generation], there should be ten nights; for a male in the fifth, six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days. (I,2, p. 222) // Par_3.9 //

In the case of the death of Bhṛgu or Agni, as well as when someone has died in a foreign land, and when a child has died or has renounced the world, immediate purification is prescribed. (I, 2, p. 223) // Par_3.10 //

If it is heard that someone who is a member of one's own lineage has died in another country, one should not observe the three-night impurity; rather, by bathing for a single day and night, one becomes pure immediately. (I,2, p. 232) // Par_3.11 //
If a Brahmin who has gone to another country meets his death due to exhaustion or the passage of time, and the lunar day [of his passing] is not known, (Parāśara Smṛti 3.12).
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on whichever eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
one should perform the offering of water, the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the ancestral rite (śrāddha).

For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb, there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water libations. (I,2, p. 237) Par_3.14.
If the fetus of a woman miscarries or is aborted, the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained. (I.2, p. 238) // Par_3.15 //

Up to the fourth month there may be a miscarriage; in the fifth and sixth months, it is a fall [of the fetus]. Beyond that, it is a birth, and for ten days there shall be impurity due to childbirth (*sūtaka*). (I,2, p. 240) // Par_3.16 //

When one who has teethed, one who has cut his first teeth, or one for whom the tonsure ceremony has been performed dies, there shall be impurity for three nights during their cremation rites. (I, 2, p. 241) // Par_3.16/1 //

Immediate purification is prescribed until the eruption of teeth; until the tonsure ceremony, it is considered to last until the night [of birth]; until the initiation into the vows, it lasts three nights; and beyond that, ten nights. (I,2, p. 243) // Par_3.17 //

For those whose householders live as celibates and in whose home the sacrificial fire is offered, there shall be no birth-impurity, nor do they engage in [worldly] contact. (I,2, p. 253) // Par_3.18 //
A Brahmin becomes defiled by contact [with impure persons] at birth as well as at death;
however, for one who has desisted from such contact, there is neither impurity due to a corpse nor impurity due to birth. (I,2, p. 254) Par_3.19 //
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, male and female slaves,
barbers, kings, and those learned in the Vedas are declared to be immediately pure.

A twice-born man who observes his vows, is purified by the Sattra sacrifice, and has maintained the sacred fires, incurs no impurity from the birth of a king, provided that the monarch so desires. (I,2, p. 255) // Par_3.21 //
When a Brahmin who has been invited for a funeral feast or a gift is distressed and ready to depart,
the sages have observed that he is purified by that very time.

But if the householder performs the *gṛhamedhin* sacrifice during the period of birth-impurity, provided he does not cause any confusion [of the rites], the mother becomes pure after ten days by bathing, while the father is pure immediately. (I,2, p. 259) Par_3.23 //
For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca); however, for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (upaspṛśya).
If a twice-born man has sexual intercourse when his wife has given birth, he incurs the impurity of birth (sūtaka), even if the Brahmin is learned in the six Vedāṅgas. (I,2, p. 260) [Par_3.25]
"Fault arises from association; indeed, there is no other fault, O twice-born one.
Therefore, a wise man should avoid association with every effort. (I,2, p. 261) // Par_3.26 //

However, during marriages, festivals, or sacrifices, if a death or birth impurity occurs in the interim, there is no fault in giving away wealth that was previously intended for distribution. (I,2, p. 262) // Par_3.27 //
If death or birth occurs again within ten days, a Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that [second period] has not yet passed its tenth day. (I,2, p. 263) Par_3.28.

For those who perish for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as for those captured while being prisoners of war, and for those who perish in battles, there is a period of impurity lasting one night. (I, 2, p. 268) // Par_3.29 //
These two persons in the world pierce the solar disc:
the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and the warrior slain while facing the enemy in battle.
Wherever a hero is slain while surrounded by enemies, he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not utter words of cowardice. (I,2, p. 269) // Par_3.31 //
Upon seeing a Brahmin who has renounced the world, the sun moves from its place: "Having pierced my orb, he shall go to the supreme station. (I,2, p. 270) // Par_3.32 //
But he who, when the armies are broken and fleeing in every direction, goes forth as their protector, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice. (I,2, p. 271) // Par_3.33 //
But for that hero whose limbs are mangled by arrows, mallets, and clubs,
celestial maidens carry him away and delight him.
Thousands of celestial nymphs run in haste toward the hero slain in battle, crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine! (I,2, p. 272). Par_3.35.
Just as the Brahmins seeking heaven go there by means of hosts of sacrifices and asceticism,
so indeed do the heroes go there in an instant, relinquishing their lives in a noble battle.
By victory one gains fortune; even by death, one obtains celestial maidens.
Since this body perishes in an instant, what anxiety can there be regarding death in battle? (I,2, p. 273) // Par_3.37 //
When blood flowing from the forehead enters the mouth in battle, it is indeed equal to the drinking of soma; this is seen as prescribed in the sacrifice of combat.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain, step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due order. (I,2, p. 274) // Par_3.39 //
For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, immediate purification is ordained through immersion in water.

Having carried and cremated a member of the highest twice-born caste who is of a different lineage, without kin, and deceased like a ghost, one becomes pure through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). (I,2, p. 275) [Par_3.41]

If one follows out of desire a deceased person, whether a relative or even a stranger, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (I,2, p. 280) // Par_3.42 //
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a deceased Kṣatriya out of ignorance, he becomes impure for one day and is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (I, 2, p. 281) // Par_3.43 //
If a Brāhmaṇa follows the corpse of a Vaiśya out of ignorance, he shall observe impurity for two nights and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (I,2, p. 282) // Par_3.44 //
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse while being carried away,
he shall remain impure for three nights.
When those three nights have passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one becomes pure by consuming clarified butter.
When the Śūdras have been turned back and have reached the water's edge, the twice-born should then follow them; this is the eternal law. (I,2, p. 283) // Par_3.47 //
[Volume II, Part 1: The Section on Expiation (Prāyaścittakāṇḍa).
If, out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or even fear, [one should act improperly]...
Whether it be a woman or a man, one should hang oneself; this is the course prescribed. (II,1, p. 18) // Par_4.1 //
Falling into blinding darkness filled with pus and blood, he enters hell for sixty thousand years. (II,1, p. 19) // Par_4.2 //

One should not cause impurity, nor the offering of water, nor the lighting of fire, nor the shedding of tears; likewise, the carriers [of the body], the givers of the fire, and those who cut the bonds [should not be mourned]. (II,1, p. 23) Parāśara 4.3.

"Purification is achieved through the Taptakṛcchra penance"—thus said Prajāpati regarding [an animal] killed by cows, or likewise one that has hanged itself, or one caused to be killed by a Brāhmaṇa. (II,1, p. 25) // Par_4.4 //
But those Brahmins who touch [the corpse], those who carry it, those who provide the fire, others who follow as attendants, and those who cut the bonds; Par_4.5.
Purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance, they should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa.
For three days one should drink warm water; for three days one should drink warm milk;
for three days one should drink warm clarified butter; and for three days one should subsist on air alone. (II,1, p. 26) // Par_4.7 //
One should drink six palas of water, three palas of milk, and one pala of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the Taptakṛcchra penance.
If a Brahmin should associate unintentionally with those who have fallen from their caste and so forth, for five days, or ten days, or even twelve days; (II,1, p. 27) // Par_4.9 //
Whether for half a month, one month, or even two months;
or for half a year, one year, or even beyond that, he remains equal to it.

In the first fortnight, one should fast for three nights; in the second, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; and in the third fortnight, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra. (II,1, p. 29) // Par_4.11 //
In the fourth case, it should be a ten-night penance; in the fifth, a *parāka* is prescribed;
in the sixth, one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*; and in the seventh, two *aindava* (or *cāndrāyaṇa*) penances.

For the sake of purification, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months during the eighth [period]; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) shall consist of gold coins in a number corresponding to the count of fortnights. (II,1, p. 30) Par_4.13.
But that woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband, goes to hell when she dies and becomes a widow again and again. (II,1, p. 33) // Par_4.14 //
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt in this matter.
She who treats her husband with contempt— whether he be poor, diseased, or foolish—
is born as a female dog after death, and again and again as a sow.
That woman who, while her husband is alive, observes a fast or undertakes a vow, takes away the lifespan of her husband; that woman shall go to hell. (Parāśara 4.17)
"And whatever vow a woman undertakes without having first asked her husband, all of that goes to the Rākṣasas; thus Manu has declared. (II.1, p. 34) // Par_4.18 //
She who behaves wickedly toward her kinsmen and relatives, or she who causes an abortion—one should never speak with such a woman at any time. (Parāśara 4.19)
Whatever sin there is in the killing of a Brahmin, that same twofold sin exists in causing an abortion;
for her, there is no expiation, and her abandonment is ordained.
Neither by the domestic fire nor by the Agnihotra sacrifice can he be purified;
he who is averse to dharma becomes a Cāṇḍāla in his actions.
If seed carried by the force of a flood sprouts in someone's field, that owner of the field receives the crop; the owner of the seed does not deserve a share. (II,1, p. 42) // Par_4.22 //
Similarly, two types of sons born of another's wife are traditionally known as the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*:
the *kuṇḍa* is one born while the husband is alive, and the *golaka* is one born when the husband is dead.
The legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the given son (*datta*), and the made son (*kṛtrimaka*):
if the mother or the father gives him away, that son becomes a "given" son (*dattaka*). (II,1, p. 48) // Par_4.24 //
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him,
the woman through whom he is superseded, as well as the giver and the officiating priest— these five all go to hell.
For the elder brother who marries before his younger brother, two *kṛcchra* penances; for the maiden, a single *kṛcchra*;
for the giver, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
There is no fault in lamenting for those who are hunchbacked, dwarfs, eunuchs, stammerers, the mentally dull, those born blind, the deaf, or the mute. (II,1, p. 51) // Par_4.27 //

There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] if he is the son of a paternal uncle, the son of a co-wife, or the son of another man's wife, provided there is a union with a wife and the sacred fire. (II,1, p. 52) // Par_4.28 //
As long as the elder brother remains, one should not perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*);
however, having obtained his permission, one may do so, according to the word of Śaṅkha.
"When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen [from his caste]—in these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. (II,1, p. 53) // Par_4.30 //
When her husband has died, the woman who remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy attains heaven upon her death, just like those who are lifelong students of sacred knowledge.
As many hairs as there are on a human being—three and a half crores—for that long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven. (II,1, p. 54) // Par_4.32 //
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so too a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoices together with him. (II,1, p. 57) // Par_4.33 //
O best of the twice-born, he who has been bitten by a wolf, a dog, a jackal, or similar creatures, should bathe and recite the Gāyatrī, the purifying mother of the Vedas. (II,1, p. 61) // Par_5.1 //
One bitten by a dog becomes pure by bathing with water from a cow's horn at the confluence of great rivers, or even by beholding the ocean.

If a twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies and the vows of initiation is bitten by a dog, he becomes pure by bathing with gold and water and consuming clarified butter. (II,1, p. 62) // Par_5.3 //
But he who, while observing a vow, has been bitten by a dog, should fast for three nights;
having drunk ghee mixed with water infused with *kuśa* grass, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
Whether he be without vows or even possessed of vows, a twice-born man who has been bitten by a dog becomes purified by prostrating himself and being gazed upon by Brahmins with their eyes.
For food that has been smelled by a dog, licked, or scratched with its claws,
washing with water is prescribed, as well as warming it over fire.
But a Brahmin woman bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf becomes pure immediately upon seeing the risen planets and stars. (Parāśara 5.7)
When the moon is never visible during the dark fortnight,
one should gaze toward whichever direction the moon has gone.
If the best of the twice-born is bitten by a dog in a village inhabited by those who are not true Brahmins,
he shall become pure immediately by circumambulating a bull and bathing.
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is killed by a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapāka, cows, or other Brahmins, or if he dies by poison or commits suicide; (II,1, p. 69) // Par_5.10 //
A Brahmin should burn that Brahmin in the world-fire (lokāgni) without the use of mantras;
likewise, having touched, carried, or burned [the corpse], he must do so in every respect among the sapinda relatives.
Thereafter, at the instruction of the Brahmins, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having taken up the burnt bones again, the twice-born man should wash them with milk. (II,1, p. 70) // Par_5.12 //

Furthermore, one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and is a twice-born (*dvija*), being impelled by time while traveling abroad, should separately cremate [the body] with his own fire according to the *Svatantra* ritual manual. (II,1, p. 71) // Par_5.13 //
"O best of sages, hear now of the funeral rites for the deceased Agnihotra performed in the house of one who has met with the destruction of his body."
Having spread out a black antelope skin, he should fashion a human figure with kuśa grass and six hundred and one stalks of palāśa flowers, including their stems.
One should place forty [beads] on the head, one hundred on the neck;
one should place one hundred on the two arms, and ten indeed on the fingers. (II,1, p. 72) // Par_5.16 //
One should place one hundred [strokes] on the buttocks, likewise two hundred on the abdomen;
one should place eight on the testicles and five on the penis.
One should offer twenty-one [oblations] for the two thighs, two hundred for the knees and shanks, and six for the toes; thereafter, one should place the sacrificial vessel.
Having placed the *śamyā* upon the penis and the *araṇī* upon the testicles,
one should place the *juhū* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left.
One should place a mortar upon the ear, set a pestle upon the back, cast a grinding stone upon the chest, and put rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds into the mouth. (Parāśara 5.20)
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* water on the ears and the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthalī*) on the eyes;
one should then place fragments of gold on the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose. (Parāśara 5.21)
One should place all the implements of the *agnihotra* there and offer a single oblation once, saying: "To this world of heaven, svāhā! (II,1, p. 73) // Par_5.22 //
Whether it be the son, a brother, or even another relative,
the wise should perform the cremation rite exactly as prescribed.
One should perform such a rite as this; it is traditionally taught that it leads to the world of Brahmā.
Those twice-born who cremate him in this manner attain the supreme goal. (II,1, p. 74) // Par_5.24 //
Driven by their own deluded intellects, they perform actions otherwise;
indeed, they become short-lived and fall into a foul hell.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the expiation for the killing of living beings, as previously declared by Parāśara and also set forth in detail in the *Manu-smṛti* (II.1, p. 77).
By killing a curlew, a crane, a swan, a ruddy goose, a cock, a web-footed bird, or a *śarabha*, one is purified in a day and night. (II,1, p. 78) // Par_6.2 //
Whether it be a crane, a lapwing, a parrot, or a pigeon, as well as one who kills snakes or crocodiles, is purified by eating only at night. (II,1, p. 79) // Par_6.3 //
One who kills wolves, crows, pigeons, francolins, or partridges is purified by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) while staying in the water during both twilights. (II,1, p. 80) // Par_6.4 //
One who kills vultures, hawks, dogs, or owls, and eats uncooked food, shall remain standing during the day and subsist on air alone for three periods of the day. (II,1, p. 81) // Par_6.5 //
One is purified from eating at night after consuming the meat of the *valguṇī*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, *kokila*, *khañjarīṭaka*, *lāvika*, and those with red wings. (II,1, p. 82) // Par_6.6 //
Having killed a kāraṇḍava duck, a cakora partridge, a piṅgala, a kurara crane, a bhāradvāja crane, or others, one becomes purified by worshipping Śiva. (II,1, p. 83) // Par_6.7 //
And for the bheruṇḍa, the blue jay, the hawk, the pigeon, and the francolin,
as well as for all other birds, there shall be a fast of one day and night.

Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a *ḍuṇḍubha* [frog], one should feed the Brahmins *kṛsara* (rice and peas) and give an iron staff as the sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 85) // Par_6.9 //
Likewise, having killed a porpoise, an iguana, a tortoise, or a porcupine, one is purified by fasting for a day and night, even if one has been eating eggplant fruit. (II,1, p. 87) // Par_6.10 //
One who kills a wolf, a jackal, a bear, a hyena, a dog, or a predator should give a *prastha* of sesame seeds to a twice-born man and subsist on air for three days. (II,1, p. 89) // Par_6.11 //
For the killing of an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, or a camel, the expiation consists of bathing at the three junctions of the day for one full day and night. (II,1, p. 90) // Par_6.12 //
One who kills a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger is purified by a three-night fast and by the libation of water to Brahmins. (II,1, p. 91) // Par_6.13 //
The slayer of a deer, a doe, or a boar, or of a sheep or a goat, shall fast for one day and night and eat only food that has not been ploughed by a furrow. (II,1, p. 92) // Par_6.14 //
In this manner, having stayed for a day and night, he should remain among all four-footed forest-dwelling creatures; indeed, he should recite the Jātavedas mantra. (II,1, p. 93) // Par_6.15 //

He who causes the death of an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman, shall perform two Prājāpatya penances and give a bull as the eleventh among ten cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 94) // Par_6.16 //
Whoever should strike a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya who is innocent, he too shall perform two Kṛcchra penances and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 95) // Par_6.17 //

Having killed a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who is devoted to ritual acts, or an excellent twice-born man who stands in improper action, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give thirty cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 105) // Par_6.18 //
If someone has killed a Caṇḍāla in the vicinity of a Brāhmaṇa, he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 106) // Par_6.19 //
If the killing of a Caṇḍāla is committed by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or indeed by anyone else, one is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance.

If a Brahmin has been struck by two thieves who are outcaste Śvapākas or Caṇḍālas, he becomes pure by bathing and consuming the five products of the cow after fasting for a day and night. (II,1, p. 107) // Par_6.21 //
If a Brahmin converses with a Śvapāka or even a Caṇḍāla, he should perform a conversation with the divine [waters] and mutter the Sāvitrī once. (II,1, p. 108) // Par_6.22 //
If one has slept together with Caṇḍālas, one should fast for three nights;
having traveled along a path used exclusively by Caṇḍālas, one becomes pure by recollecting the Gāyatrī.
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun;
upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. (II,1, p. 109) // Par_6.24 //
If the eldest brother drinks water from wells or ponds dug by Caṇḍālas out of ignorance, he becomes pure after one day and night of eating only a single meal. (II,1, p. 111) // Par_6.25 //
Having drunk water from a well that has been touched by the vessel of a Caṇḍāla, one attains purification after three nights of subsisting on cow urine and barley gruel. (II,1, p. 112) // Par_6.26 //
If a twice-born man drinks water that has been contained in a jar belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance if he discards it at that very moment.
If one does not discharge water [from the penis] while the food in his body is still undigested, the Prājāpatya penance should not be given; instead, he should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
A Brahmin shall perform the Sāṃtapana penance; a Kṣatriya, the Prājāpatya; a Vaiśya shall perform half of that, and a Śūdra shall perform a quarter of it. (II,1, p. 113) // Par_6.29 //

If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk contained in a vessel belonging to the lowest castes (antyaja), [he must undergo penance]. (II,1, p. 114) // Par_6.30 //
For the twice-born, atonement is achieved through the Brahmakūrca fast;
for a Śūdra, it is through fasting and likewise through giving according to his capacity.

If a most excellent twice-born man should ever eat the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance, he becomes pure after ten nights of subsisting on cow's urine and barley gruel. (II,1, p. 115) // Par_6.32 //
One should eat a single morsel at a time of cow-urine and barley-gruel; for one who remains under this restraint for ten days, that is designated as the vow. (II,1, p. 116) Par_6.33.
But where a Caṇḍāla remains in a house unrecognized, O twice-born ones, once he is known, the twice-born show favor to one who has approached them with devotion. (II,1, p. 118) Par_6.34 //
Those who have mastered the Vedas, chanting the teachings issued from the mouth of the Sage,
shall rescue him as he falls from the mixture of evil, for they are knowers of the Dharma.
He should eat barley-gruel with curds, ghee, milk, and cow-urine, and he should perform ablutions at all three junctions of the day. (II,1, p. 119) // Par_6.36 //
For three days one should eat with curd, for three days one should eat with clarified butter,
and for three days one should eat with milk— spending three days on each one respectively.
One should not eat food that is corrupted by intention, nor that which is leftover, nor that which is infested with worms;
[as for milk products], one may consume three palas of curd and milk, but only one pala of ghee. (II,1, p. 120) // Par_6.38 //
Purification for both copper and bell-metal is achieved with ash;
for garments, by washing with water; and for earthenware, by discarding it.
Having placed safflower, molasses, cotton, salt, oil,
and clarified butter at the door, one should place grains and fire within the house.
Having thus become purified, he should thereafter perform the satiation of Brahmins;
he should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins. (II.1, p. 121) // Par_6.41 //
Furthermore, it is purified by plastering, digging, fire-offerings, and recitation;
and for Brahmins, no defect of the ground exists when the site has been properly prepared.
If one has contact with Caṇḍālas for a month or even for half a month, one becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel. (II,1, p. 122) // Par_6.43 //
A washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter, or a basket-weaver may dwell unrecognized in the house of one belonging to the four castes. (II,1, p. 123) // Par_6.44 //
Having understood this, one should perform the expiation even for half of what was previously stated;
one should not set fire to the house, but should carry out all the rest. (II,1, p. 124) // Par_6.45 //
If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone’s house,
he must be expelled from that dwelling, and the earthenware vessels must be discarded.
One should never discard a vessel that is full of liquid;
likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
If a worm should arise in the opening of a wound of a Brahmin where pus and blood have formed, what expiation shall there be for him? (II,1, p. 126) // Par_6.48 //
By bathing for three days and drinking the urine, dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter of cows, one who has been defiled by worms shall become pure.
A Kṣatriya, having given five māṣas of gold,
should likewise prescribe a cow as the sacrificial fee for a Vaiśya, along with a fast.
For Śūdras there should be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts. "It is flawless"—this is the statement that the gods of the earth utter. (II,1, p. 127) // Par_6.51 //

Having bowed with one's head, that [gift] should indeed be accepted, for it yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; it fills whatever gap there may be in recitation, whatever gap in austerity, and whatever gap in the performance of sacrificial rites. (II,1, p. 128) // Par_6.52 //
Everything provided by the Brahmins becomes flawless,
even in times of disease, calamity, exhaustion, famine, or civil unrest.
Fasting, vows, and burnt offerings are indeed accomplished by the twice-born;
or rather, when the Brahmins are satisfied, they bestow all grace. (II,1, p. 129) // Par_6.54 //
One obtains all desires here through those things provided by the twice-born;
likewise, favor is prescribed for the weak, as well as for children and the elderly. (II,1, p. 130) // Par_6.55 //
Otherwise, there would be a fault; therefore, it is not considered a favor.
Whether out of affection, or greed, or fear, or even from ignorance—(II,1, p. 131) // Par_6.56 //
But those who show favor [to such a person], that sin goes to them; for they say that when the end of the body has arrived, one must observe the prescribed rule. (II,1, p. 132) Par_6.57
One who is healthy should never [omit a meal] due to the obstruction of a great task;
those fools who do so for one who is healthy speak what is unregulated. (II,1, p. 133) Par_6.58
Those who create obstacles for him fall into a foul hell—
he who, having himself undertaken a vow, treats a Brahmin with contempt.
His fast would be in vain, and he would not be endowed with merit;
that very rule alone is to be accepted if even a single twice-born man should say so. (II,1, p. 134) // Par_6.60 //
One should indeed follow the word of the twice-born; otherwise, one becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
For Brahmins are a moving sacred ford (tīrtha), and the virtuous are indeed the very embodiment of sacred fords.
By the water of their words alone, defiled people are purified; whatever the Brāhmaṇas speak, the gods consider that to be true. (II,1, p. 135) // Par_6.62 //
A Brahmin embodies all the gods; his word is never otherwise.
Fasting, religious observances, ritual bathing, pilgrimage to sacred fords, the recitation of mantras, and austerity—(II,1, p. 136) // Par_6.63 //
The fruit belongs entirely to him for whom the rite has been properly performed by the Brahmins.
[However, this applies when] the food is infested with insects or defiled by flies and hair. (Parāśara 6.64)
If he should touch water during that interval, he should touch that food with ashes;
and the Brahmin who, while eating, touches his foot with his hand [should likewise touch it with ashes].
He eats his own leavings from the hand once the vessel has been set aside;
he should not eat while standing on sandals, nor even while seated upon a couch. (II,1, p. 138) Par_6.66 //
One should avoid eating food that has been seen by a dog or a Caṇḍāla;
likewise, one should observe the purification of food that is otherwise prohibited.
Just as it was stated by Parāśara, so do I say to you:
"Food cooked from a drona or an āḍhaka measure that has been defiled by crows or dogs. (II,1, p. 139) // Par_6.68 //

One should inform the Brāhmaṇas, "By what means shall this be purified? However, one should not discard a *droṇa* measure of food that has been licked by a crow or a dog. (II,1, p. 140) // Par_6.69 //
A *droṇa* is known by Brahmins who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and who follow the treatises on Dharma as being thirty-two *prasthas*; two *prasthas* are remembered as an *āḍhaka*.

Therefore, those who know the Śruti and Smṛti understand that food from a droṇa or an āḍhaka measure [is pure], even if it has been licked by a crow or a dog, or smelled by a cow or a donkey. (II,1, p. 141) // Par_6.71 //

A Brahmin should discard even a small amount of food; purification occurs when the quantity is one *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka*. One should remove from the food that portion which has been touched by saliva. (II,1, p. 142) // Par_6.72 //
Having sprinkled it with golden water, one should heat it with fire;
thus it is touched by both fire and golden water.
Through the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins, food becomes pure at that very moment;
but how can there be purification for oil or even cow’s milk in that situation? (II,1, p. 144) // Par_6.74 //
In that case, one should discard a small portion and purify it by straining out the fat;
the purification of dairy products is prescribed by means of the flame of fire.

**Purification of Substances:** Now, therefore, follows the purification of substances according to the words of Parāśara: "The purification of wooden vessels is held to be by planing. (II,1, p. 147) // Par_7.1 //
Bell-metal is purified by ashes, copper is purified by acid;
a woman who does not have intercourse with a man is purified by her menses. (II,1, p. 150) // Par_7.2 //
A river is purified by its current if no contamination is visible; but how can large wells, small wells, or ponds be purified when they have been somehow defiled? (II,1, p. 153) // Par_7.3 //
Having indeed drawn out a hundred jars [of water], one is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
A girl of eight years is *Gaurī*, while one of nine years is *Rohiṇī*. (II,1, p. 156) // Par_7.4 //
A girl becomes a maiden at ten years of age, and after that she is subject to menstruation;
but when the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter [is at fault]. (II,1, p. 157) // Par_7.5 //
Month after month, her own fathers—the mother, the father, and likewise the eldest brother—drink her menstrual blood themselves. (II,1, p. 158) Par_7.6.
Three go to hell upon seeing a menstruating girl:
he who would marry such a girl, and the Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by pride, weds her.

For that Brahmin who, being twice-born, indulges in the company of a Vṛṣalī for even a single night becomes unfit to converse with and excluded from the ritual row; he is a husband of a Vṛṣalī. (II,1, p. 159) Par_7.8 //
Subsisting on alms and reciting prayers constantly, he is purified in three years;
likewise when, after the sun has set, he [accidentally touches] a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or a woman.
And how is purification prescribed for one who touches a woman who has recently given birth?
[It is attained] by looking at fire, gold, and the path of the moon. (Parāśara 7.10)

And having been permitted by a Brāhmaṇa, she becomes pure after performing a ritual bath; likewise, when two Brāhmaṇa women who are menstruating have touched one another. (II,1, p. 160) // Par_7.11 //
She should remain without food for that long; by three nights alone she is purified, having touched one another while in their menstrual flow, whether she be a Brāhmaṇī or a Kṣatriyā.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, touch one another, the former shall perform half a kṛcchra penance and the latter one quarter.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another, the former shall perform a penance of three-quarters, while the latter shall perform a penance of one-quarter.
A Śūdra woman is purified by a penance; she is purified by a gift.
A menstruating woman who has bathed is purified on the fourth day. (II,1, p. 164) // Par_7.15 //
One should perform rites for the gods, the ancestors, and so forth upon the cessation of the menstrual flow;
however, that flow which occurs daily in women due to illness [is not subject to this restriction]. (II,1, p. 165) // Par_7.16 //
Therefore, she is not impure; for that reason, it is considered that [the period] lasts until the end of the day.
As long as the flow of blood continues, she shall not be one of virtuous conduct. (II,1, p. 168) // Par_7.17 //
Indeed, when her menses have ceased, a woman may be approached for household duties;
yet on the first day she is like a Caṇḍālī, and on the second day she is a slayer of a Brahmin.
On the third day she is called a washerwoman, and on the fourth day she becomes pure;
for when impurity arises from childbirth, one who is not afflicted must bathe ten times.

Having bathed repeatedly, he should touch him; then that afflicted twice-born man shall become pure, even if he has been touched by one who is impure from food remnants, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra. (II,1, p. 170) // Par_7.20 //
Having fasted for one night, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Upon being touched by a Śūdra who is not rendered impure by food remnants, bathing is prescribed. (II,1, p. 171) // Par_7.21 //
If one is touched by the leavings of another, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance;
bell-metal is purified by ashes, provided it is not stained by liquor. (II,1, p. 172) // Par_7.22 //

Objects touched by even a trace of liquor are purified by scrubbing with fire and stones; likewise, bronze vessels that have been smelled by a cow or defiled by dogs and crows [are purified in the same manner]. (II,1, p. 172) Par_7.23.
Those items that have been defiled by the leavings of a Śūdra, as well as those used for rinsing the mouth or washing the feet in a bell-metal vessel, are purified by ten alkaline substances.
Having cast [the metal] into the ground for six months and then extracted it, one should bring it back;
this is the purification of iron and iron-based items, as well as lead, in fire. (II,1, p. 173) // Par_7.25 //
One should wash with water these items: ivory, bone, horn, silver, golden vessels, and bowls made of gems or stone. (II,1, p. 174) // Par_7.26 //
Furthermore, for stone, purification is declared to be by scrubbing;
for earthenware, purification is by burning; and for grains, it is also by winnowing. (II,1, p. 176) // Par_7.27 //
The purification of bamboo, bark, rags, linen, cotton garments, woolen cloth, and silk fabrics is held to be achieved by sprinkling them with water. (II,1, p. 179) // Par_7.28 //
For items made of muñja grass, equipment, winnowing baskets, hemp, fruits, skins, straw, wood, and ropes, sprinkling with water is prescribed. (II,1, p. 181) // Par_7.29 //
Cushions such as tuḷikās and items such as red garments attain purity by being dried in the sun and then sprinkled with water. (II,1, p. 184) // Par_7.30 //

Manu has declared that cats, flies, insects, moths, worms, and frogs do not cause one to become impure from the remnants of food, even when they touch what is pure or impure. (II,1, p. 185) // Par_7.31 //

Water that has reached the ground, as well as mutual droplets [from the mouth], food remnants, and oily substances—Manu has declared these not to be "leavings" (ucchiṣṭa). (II.1, p. 186) // Par_7.32 //

According to the Dharma, they know that there is no such thing as "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) in the case of betel, sugarcane, fruit, oil used after a meal, anointing ointment, the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), and the Soma juice.
Roads, mud, water, boats, paths, and grass—
as well as structures built of baked bricks— are purified by wind and the sun.
A continuous stream that is not defiled, dust raised by the wind, women, the elderly, and children—these are never considered impure. (II,1, p. 188) // Par_7.35 //

In the event of the ruin of one's country, during exile, or even amidst diseases and calamities, one must certainly protect one's own body and so forth; thereafter, one should practice the Dharma. (II,1, p. 196) // Par_7.36 //
By whatever means possible—whether mild or harsh—one should rescue oneself from degradation; once capable, one should practice the Dharma. (II,1, p. 197) // Par_7.37 //
But once the time of calamity has passed, one should attend to the rules of purity and conduct;
thereafter, having restored one's own purification, being established in well-being, one should practice the Dharma.
If death should occur unintentionally while cows are being bound with their tethering ropes, what expiation shall there be for a sin committed unintentionally? (II,1, p. 199) // Par_8.1 //
He should confess his own sin to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who understand the treatises on Dharma, and who are devoted to their own duties. (II,1, p. 205) // Par_8.2 //

Those Brahmins who, through ignorance, perform agriculture while neglecting the Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī, the twilight devotions, and the fire-rituals, are mere bearers of the name. (II,1, p. 207) Par_8.3 //
"Among those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on their birth alone—even if they assemble by the thousands—there exists no status as an assembly. (II,1, p. 209) // Par_8.4 //
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, proclaim as such, that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it. (II,1, p. 210) // Par_8.5 //
He who prescribes an expiation without having understood the treatises on Dharma becomes purified by that very expiation, while the guilt falls upon the assembly.
Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas may declare, that should be known as Dharma, and not that which is proclaimed by thousands of others. (II,1, p. 212) // Par_8.7 //
Evil recoils from those who proclaim the Dharma while seeking the path of valid cognition, for they speak of qualities that truly exist.
Just as water situated within a stone is purified by the wind and the sun, so too shall his misdeed be destroyed through the command of the assembly. (II,1, p. 213) // Par_8.9 //
It goes neither to the doer nor to the assembly;
through contact with wind, the sun, and so forth, evil perishes like water. (II,1, p. 214) // Par_8.10 //
Whether they be four or even three Brahmins who possess knowledge of the Vedas, maintain the sacred fires, and are capable, that assembly is so designated. (II,1, p. 215) // Par_8.11 //
Those others who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet are masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
whether five or three such persons who know the Dharma— that is proclaimed to be an assembly (pariṣad).
Even a single person among sages who know the self, among the twice-born who perform sacrifices, and among those who have completed their Vedic vows, may constitute an assembly.
Five [types of assemblies] were previously mentioned by me; in their absence, there are three: that assembly is proclaimed as one where members are content with their own livelihood. Par_8.14.
But beyond this, those brahmins who are merely bearers of the name—there is no status as an assembly among them, even if they number in the thousands. (II,1, p. 218) // Par_8.15 //
Just as an elephant made of wood, or a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
As a village site is empty, as a well is without water, and as an oblation offered where there is no fire, so is a Brahmin who lacks the sacred mantras. (II,1, p. 219) // Par_8.17 //

Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a saline field is fruitless [for cultivation], and just as a gift given to one who lacks knowledge is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. (II,1, p. 220) // Par_8.18 //
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by means of many parts, so too is Brahminhood [attained] through consecrations preceded by mantras. (II,1, p. 221) Par_8.19 //
Those twice-born men who, being mere bearers of the name, prescribe penance—they, being performers of sinful deeds, went together to hell. (Parāśara 8.20)

Those twice-born who recite the Veda and those who are devoted to the five sacrifices rescue the three worlds, even if they are devoted to the pleasures of the five senses. (II,1, p. 222) // Par_8.21 //
A well-kindled fire blazing in the cremation grounds is a consumer of all things;
likewise, a Brahmin learned in the Vedas is a deity, even if he consumes all things. (II,1, p. 224) // Par_8.22 //
Just as all impurities are cast into water, so too should one cast all evil into the fire of the twice-born. (II,1, p. 227) // Par_8.23 //
A Brahmin devoid of the Gāyatrī becomes more impure even than a Śūdra;
those twice-born ones who know the true essence of the Gāyatrī and Brahman are honored by people.
Even a twice-born man of immoral conduct is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses;
for who would abandon a wicked cow to milk a well-behaved she-ass? (II,1, p. 228) // Par_8.25 //

The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas, whatever they may declare—even in jest—that is remembered as the supreme Dharma. (II,1, p. 229) // Par_8.26 //

One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), a reciter of the Dharma, and the three principal orders of life—this assembly consists of at least ten members. (II,1, p. 230) // Par_8.27 //
Remaining with the king’s permission, one should prescribe the penance;
it must not be performed by oneself alone, but a small expiation should be carried out [under his supervision]. (II,1, p. 232) // Par_8.28 //
Whatever sin a king commits by transgressing against those Brahmins whom he intends to harm, that sin becomes tenfold and follows after the king. (II,1, p. 233) // Par_8.29 //
One should always offer an expiation in front of a temple of the deities;
then, having performed the *ātmakṛcchra* penance, one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas (*vedamātṛ*).
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should bathe at the three junctions of the day;
he should dwell among cows at night and follow after them during the day. (II,1, p. 237) // Par_8.31 //

Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (II,1, p. 238) // Par_8.32 //
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking milk. (Pariccheda 8.33)
One should drink water when they are drinking, and lie down when they are lying down;
one should rescue with all one's strength a wife who has fallen or is mired in the mud. (II,1, p. 239) // Par_8.34 //
He who would sacrifice his life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin; he is a protector of both the cow and the Brahmin.
One should prescribe a Prājāpatya penance corresponding to the killing of a cow;
one should then divide that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra into four kinds. (II,1, p. 240) // Par_8.36 //
For one day he eats a single meal; for one day he eats only at night;
for one day he eats food that is unasked for; and for one day he subsists on air alone.
For two days he should eat but one meal a day, for two days he should take a single meal,
for two days he should be one who does not beg, and for two days he should subsist on air alone.
For three days he should eat a single meal a day, for three days he should eat only at night,
for three days he should not beg for food, and for three days he should subsist on air alone.

For four days he should eat a single meal a day; for four days he should eat only at night; for four days he should not beg for food; and for four days he should subsist on air alone. (II,1, p. 241) // Par_8.40 //
Then, once the penance has been performed, he should provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas;
he should give sacrificial fees to the learned priests and the twice-born should recite purificatory prayers.
But having fed the Brahmins, the cow-killer is purified; of this there is no doubt.
For the sake of protecting cattle, one shall not incur sin through their confinement or tethering;
however, one should recognize that killing them depends on whether it was done intentionally or unintentionally. (II,1, p. 255) // Par_9.1 //

If, after striking with a staff, one should cause [the cow] to fall by means of another blow, then the penance prescribed for killing a cow should be performed twice over. (II,1, p. 256) // Par_9.2 //
Imprisonment, confinement, the yoke, and execution constitute the fourfold [punishment].
For imprisonment, one should perform one quarter of the penance; for confinement, two quarters. (II,1, p. 257) // Par_9.3 //
If [a cow] falls while being tied with a tether, he should perform penance reduced by one quarter;
this applies to the case of its falling in a cow-pen, a house, a difficult pass, or on uneven ground. (II,1, p. 258) Par_9.4 //

Furthermore, when cows die in rivers, in the oceans, or in other places—provided it is not at the mouth of a river—and in a burnt region, this is called *stambhana* (obstruction) due to the blocking [of the flow]. (II,1, p. 259) // Par_9.5 //
Whether in the house or in the forest, if a cow should die while bound by a tether, a rope, a halter, or ornaments such as necklaces and jewelry; ||| 9.6 ||

One should know that very same thing to be bondage, whether it is committed through desire or without desire; such as when one is oppressed by men with a plow, a cart, a line [of oxen], or on their back. (II,1, p. 260) // Par_9.7 //
The owner of the ox incurs death; the rope is the cause of its slaughter.
Whether intoxicated, careless, insane, conscious, or unconscious—(II,1, p. 261) // Par_9.8 //
One who commits an act of violence out of lust or anger should be struck with staffs or stones;
whether he is wounded or even killed, for that [intention] is indeed the cause of the downfall.
As thick as a thumb and a cubit in length, moist and with its leaves intact—this is designated as the staff (daṇḍa). (II,1, p. 262) // Par_9.10 //
Whether he has fainted and fallen, or has been struck with a staff,
when he rises and walks five, seven, or ten paces, [he is purified].
If he should take a mouthful of food or even drink water, provided he was previously afflicted by disease, no expiation is required. (II,1, p. 263) // Par_9.12 //

Having killed an insentient embryo, one vow is prescribed: one quarter [of the penance] when it is in the form of a mass, two quarters when it is comparable to a fetus, and three-quarters when it has reached term.
For an offense involving one-quarter [of a limb], there shall be the shaving of the body hair; for two-quarters, the beard as well;
for three-quarters, everything except the top-knot; but for a fatal blow, including the top-knot. (II,1, p. 264) Par_9.14.
For one-quarter of the penance, a pair of garments; for one-half, a brass vessel;
for three-quarters, one should give a bull; and for the fourth part, two cows are prescribed.
But if he is seen with all his limbs fully formed and endowed with consciousness, complete in every major and minor limb, he should perform the cow-vow twice over. (II,1, p. 265) // Par_9.16 //
If a cow is struck with a stone or a staff such that its horn is broken, one should perform the penance of one quarter-pāda; if its eye is damaged, two pādas. (II,1, p. 266) [Parāśara 9.17]

For striking the tail, one should perform a quarter-penance; for breaking a bone, two quarters; for cutting off an ear, three quarters; and for causing death, one should perform the entire penance. (II,1, p. 267) // Par_9.18 //
In the case of a broken horn, a broken bone, or likewise a broken hip, if he survives for six months, no penance is required. (II,1, p. 268) // Par_9.19 //
When the wound has healed, one should apply an oil massage with the hand, and fodder should be provided until the horse has regained its full strength. (Parivrajaka 9.20)
As long as all its limbs are complete, so long should a man nourish it; having bowed before a Brahmin in the form of a cow, he should release it. (II,1, p. 269) // Par_9.21 //
If, however, his body were incomplete with missing limbs,
then one should prescribe an expiation for that cow-slayer on his behalf.
One who, being arrogant, kills a cow by force using wood, clods of earth, stones, or even a weapon—for him, one should prescribe purification. (II,1, p. 270) [Parāśara 9.23]
One should perform the Sāṃtapana penance for killing a wooden post, the Prājāpatya for a clod of earth,
the Taptakṛcchra for a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for a weapon.
In the *saṃtapanakṛcchra*, there are five cows; likewise, three in the *prājāpatya*;
in the *taptakṛcchra*, there are eight; and in the *atikṛcchra*, thirteen.
"In the case of killing living beings, one should provide a substitute for them, or pay its equivalent value; so Manu has declared. (Parāśara 9.26)

Except for branding or marking, and likewise for the purpose of transport or release, as well as for the sake of protection at night, there is no offense in confining or binding [the animal] (II,1, p. 271). // Par_9.27 //

In cases of excessive burning, excessive carrying, as well as piercing the nose, or transporting [the animal] across rivers and mountains, one should prescribe an expiation. (II,1, p. 272) // Par_9.28 //

In the case of excessive burning, one should perform a quarter-penance; for carrying [the load], one should perform two quarters; for [burning] on the nose, one should perform three-quarters; but for causing a fall, one should perform the entire penance.
"But if an ox, bound by its yoke-halter, perishes from exhaustion, it has been stated by Parāśara himself that [the penance] is one quarter according to the rule" (II,1, p. 273). (Parāśara 9.30)
Confinement, binding, carrying loads, striking, driving through difficult terrain, and the use of a yoke— these are the six causes of death.
If a cow or a beast dies while its limbs are well-secured by a tethering rope within the house, the owner shall be considered guilty; he deserves half of the penance. (II,1, p. 274) // Par_9.32 //
Cows should not be tied with coconut fibers, nor with hemp, nor even with muñja grass, nor with cords made of bark; even when they have been tied, one should remain standing there holding an axe.
One should bind the sacrificial animal facing south with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass;
there is no expiation for [the animal] burnt by fire caught in the tethering rope. (II,1, p. 276) // Par_9.34 //
If there should be wood in that place, what would be the expiation?
By reciting the purifying goddess, one is released from the sin therein.

By driving [cattle] into wells or ponds, by causing them to fall during the felling of trees, or by selling them as fodder for oxen, one thereby incurs the sin of killing a cow. (II,1, p. 277) // Par_9.36 //
But when someone who has been propitiated should fall into a different state— whether his hearing and heart are shattered, or he is submerged in the perilous depths of a well— (Pariccheda 9.37)
If he dies there from climbing out of a well, or if his neck or feet are broken,
one should perform three-quarters of the penance.
For those who perish in the excavation of a well, in the embankment of a tank, in the damming of a river,
at water-stations, or in [other] waters, no penance is prescribed.
In the case of digging a well, a pond, or likewise a large excavation, as well as other excavations made for religious merit, no expiation is prescribed. (II,1, p. 279) // Par_9.40 //
One should prescribe an expiation for any man who desires to dig a pit at the door of a house or in his dwellings, whether for his own business or for the excavation of a house.
For those who die at night while imprisoned, those killed by snakes or tigers, and those perished by fire or lightning, no expiation is prescribed. (II,1, p. 280) // Par_9.42 //
In the case of those killed by a shower of arrows during a village raid, by the collapse of their houses, or by excessive rain, no penance is prescribed. (II,1, p. 281) // Par_9.43 //
For those killed in battle, those burned in their homes, and those perished in forest fires or village destructions, no expiation is prescribed. (II,1, p. 282) // Par_9.44 //
If a cow is restrained for the purpose of medical treatment or to deliver a dead fetus,
and she dies despite efforts being made, no expiation is required.

One should prescribe an expiation for the death of many beings, or for their imprisonment or confinement, as well as for the improper treatment administered by a physician. (II,1, p. 284) // Par_9.46 //
And in the event of a calamity involving bulls, as many people as are present as spectators shall incur sin, provided they do not attempt to prevent it. (II,1, p. 285) // Par_9.47 //

When one person is killed by many acting together, and it is not known whose blow caused the death, the slayer must be identified through divine means and brought back by those appointed by the king. (II,1, p. 286) // Par_9.48 //
If some single woman is killed by several people through fate,
they shall each perform separately a quarter of the penance for killing, one for each.
If blood is seen, it indicates hatred; one afflicted by disease becomes emaciated;
saliva is present in those who have been bitten—thus should the investigation proceed.
"Even when urged for the sake of food, he does not go on a journey;
thus it was said by Manu alone, who knew all the scriptures. (II,1, p. 288) [Parāśara 9.51]
But the expiation prescribed by him is that a cow-killer shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
for the sake of preserving his hair, he shall perform double the vow. (II,1, p. 290) // Par_9.52 //
When a vow is prescribed as being twofold, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be twofold;
this applies whether it be a king, a prince, or a Brāhmaṇa who is deeply learned.
If one has not performed the shaving [of the head], one should prescribe an expiation:
having pulled out all the hair, one should cut off two finger-breadths. (II,1, p. 291) // Par_9.54 //

Thus, the shaving of the head for women and young girls is prescribed; however, for a woman, there is neither the cutting off of hair nor staying or eating at a distance [from her husband]. (II,1, p. 292) // Par_9.55 //
One should not stay in a cow-pen at night, nor should one follow the cows during the day,
especially in rivers, at river-confluences, and in forests.
Women should not wear deerskin as clothing; rather, they should observe their vows alone.
It is prescribed that they bathe at the three junctions of the day and likewise perform the worship of the gods. (II,1, p. 293) // Par_9.57 //
In the midst of their kinsmen, they should observe vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa;
remaining constantly in their homes, they should remain pure and practice their religious observances.
In this world, he who, having committed the slaughter of a cow, desires to conceal it, goes without doubt to the terrible hell Kālasūtra. (II,1, p. 294) // Par_9.59 //
Released from that hell,
that man is born in the world of mortals for seven lifetimes as one who is impotent, miserable, and afflicted with leprosy.
Therefore, one should disclose one's sin and constantly practice one's own duty;
one should avoid excessive anger toward women, children, servants, cows, and Brahmins.

I shall declare the beneficial expiation for all the four castes; for purification after approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (II,1, p. 297) // Par_10.1 //
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (II,1, p. 298) // Par_10.2 //
One should indeed determine the size of a morsel to be equal to a hen’s egg;
otherwise, due to the fault of improper disposition, there is neither dharma nor purification. (II,1, p. 304) // Par_10.3 //

Once the penance has been performed, one should then provide a meal for Brahmins; one should give two cows and a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins. (II,1, p. 305) // Par_10.4 //
If a twice-born man approaches a Caṇḍāla woman or a Śvapāka woman,
he must fast for three nights according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
Having let the wind blow upon his topknot, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give two cows as a sacrificial fee; Pārāśara has declared this to be purification. (II,1, p. 306) Par_10.6.
If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya has sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give away two pairs of cattle. (II,1, p. 307) // Par_10.7 //
If a Śūdra has sexual intercourse with a Śvapākī or a Caṇḍālī woman,
he shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give four pairs of cattle.
If, however, he should approach his mother, or likewise his sister or his own daughter, having approached these while deluded, he shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (II,1, p. 311) // Par_10.9 //

One should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; one is purified by the cutting off of the penis. The same applies to sexual intercourse with a mother’s sister, which requires the excision of one's own male organ. (II,1, p. 316) // Par_10.10 //
"But he who should go [to her] through ignorance shall perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances and give ten pairs of cattle; Pārāśara has declared this to be purification. (II,1, p. 317) // Par_10.11 //

Having ascended to the wives of his father, or a brother’s daughter who is a relative of his mother, or likewise the wife of his teacher, his daughter-in-law, and the wife of his brother; (II,1, p. 319) // Par_10.12 //

If one approaches the wife of a maternal uncle or a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā), one should perform three Prājāpatya penances; one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee, and one is purified—of this there is no doubt.

Having approached a female animal for sexual intercourse, or likewise a female buffalo, a camel, a female monkey, a female donkey, or a female pig, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow. (II,1, p. 339) // Par_10.14 //

One who has had sexual intercourse with a cow is purified by three nights if he gives a single cow to a Brāhmaṇa; however, one who has had intercourse with a female buffalo, a camel, a she-ass, or a female dog is purified in a day and a night. (II,1, p. 342) // Par_10.15 //
In a riot or in battle, during famine or in the destruction of people,
or when captured as a prisoner or afflicted by fear, one should always look upon one's own wife.
A woman who maintains contact with Caṇḍālas should, after having invited ten excellent Brahmins, disclose her own transgression. (II,1, p. 343) // Par_10.17 //
Standing in a pit dug up to her neck, filled with cow-dung, water, and mud,
she should remain there without food and emerge after a full day and night.
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should eat a meal of barley-gruel;
after fasting for three nights, he should dwell in water for one night.
Having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper together with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should drink the water.
Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
as long as she performs that vow, she remains living outside [the community]. (II,1, p. 344) // Par_10.21 //
Once the penance has been performed, one should then provide a feast for Brahmins; Pārāśara declared that purity is attained by giving two cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 345) // Par_10.22 //
For women of the four castes, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa vows [are prescribed];
as is the earth, so is a woman; therefore, one should not defile her. (II,1, p. 346) // Par_10.23 //
"If she has been enjoyed by a robber who has killed and bound her by force out of fear, she becomes pure by performing the *sāṃtapana* penance; so said Pārāśara. (II,1, p. 347) // Par_10.24 //
But a woman who has been enjoyed once against her will by those of sinful deeds shall be purified by the Prājāpatya penance and by the flow of menses.
Half of the body of that man falls [with him] whose wife drinks liquor;
