for one whose half-body has fallen, no atonement is prescribed. (II,1, p. 349) // Par_10.26 //

While muttering the Gāyatrī, one should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance, consisting of cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with Kuśa grass. (II,1, p. 351) // Par_10.27 //
A fast for one night is recorded as the *sāṃtapana* penance.
[If she] should conceive a child by a paramour when her husband is dead, missing, or has departed [for a long journey], (II,1, p. 352) // Par_10.28 //

Others should abandon her in another kingdom, for she is fallen and a doer of evil; but when a Brāhmaṇa woman goes forth united with another man, [she must be abandoned]. (II,1, p. 354) // Par_10.29 //
She, however, is declared lost; there is no return for her who, out of delusion and desire, departs having abandoned her kinsmen, sons, and husband. (II,1, p. 356) // Par_10.30 //
But that woman, having fallen into intoxication and delusion, and being struck with sticks and other weapons out of anger, is lost in the next world, especially among human beings.
If she has departed as one who is not to return, there is no expiation once the tenth day has arrived. (II,1, p. 358) // Par_10.32 //
For ten days one should not abandon the wife; likewise, one should abandon her if she has lost her sense of hearing.
The husband shall perform the Kṛcchra penance, and his kinsmen half a Kṛcchra.

Having eaten and drunk with them, one is purified after a day and night; but when a Brāhmaṇī woman, being free from [the protection of] another man, has sexual intercourse [with such a person], she is likewise purified. (II,1, p. 359) // Par_10.34 //
Having gone [to another], she passes through a hundred men; her kinsmen should abandon her.
If she should go to the house of a man, that house would become impure. (II,1, p. 360) // Par_10.35 //
That which is the husband's mother's house is indeed the house of the paramour;
having smeared that house with cow-dung, one should afterwards sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should discard an earthen vessel and purify cloth and wood;
one should purify all ritual materials, including those made from fruit, using cow-hair.
Copper vessels [should be purified] with the five products of the cow, and bell-metal vessels with ashes ten times over;
the Brahmin should perform the expiation as prescribed by the Brahmins.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee and perform two Prājāpatya penances;
for the others, purification consists of fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are purified by fasts, meritorious vows, ritual bathing, twilight devotions, worship, and so forth, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, compassion, and gifts. (II,1, p. 361) // Par_10.40 //
Space, wind, fire, and water on the earth are pure;
likewise, sacrificial grass (darbha) is not defiled in sacrifices, just as the ritual cups (camasa) are not.
If a Brahmin has consumed impure semen, beef, or even the food of a Caṇḍāla, he shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (II,1, p. 364) // Par_11.1 //
In the same way, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should perform half a Cāndrāyaṇa;
and when a Śūdra eats likewise, he should perform a Prājāpatya penance. (II,1, p. 374) // Par_11.2 //
A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); a twice-born man (dvija) should drink the Brahmakūrca;
or they should respectively give one, two, three, or four cows to a Brāhmaṇa and the others in order.

The food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity, and the food of one whose food is not to be eaten; food that is suspected [of being forbidden], prohibited food, and likewise the leavings of another—(II,1, p. 375) // Par_11.4 //
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food] out of ignorance or due to distress, he should perform the purifying Brahmakūrca penance once he becomes aware of it. Parāśara 11.5.
When food has been defiled by children, mongooses, or cats, it becomes pure after being sprinkled with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water; of this there is no doubt. (II,1, p. 390) // Par_11.6 //
When Brahmins are seated in a single row eating together, if even one should set aside his vessel, one must not have the remaining food eaten. (II,1, p. 398) // Par_11.7 //
If a Brahmin should eat from that row where food is being consumed as leavings out of delusion,
he must perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Sāṃtapana penance.
Milk, white garlic, eggplant, the *gṛñjana* plant, onion, tree resin, and mushrooms (II,1, p. 399). // Par_11.9 //
If a twice-born man consumes camel’s milk or ewe’s milk through ignorance,
he becomes pure by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having eaten a frog as well as the flesh of a mouse, a Brahmin, knowing this, is purified by subsisting on barley-gruel for a day and a night. (II,1, p. 405) // Par_11.11 //

A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are diligent in their duties and pure in their vows—food from their houses may always be eaten by the twice-born at rites for the gods and the ancestors. (II,1, p. 410) // Par_11.12 //
Clarified butter, oil, as well as milk and food cooked with fat—if a Brahmin goes to the bank of a river and eats these, he partakes of the food of a Śūdra. (II,1, p. 411) Par_11.13 //
A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is constantly addicted to liquor and meat and who engages in base occupations, as if he were a dog-cooker. (II,1, p. 416) // Par_11.14 //
A twice-born man should not abandon those Śūdras who are devoted to serving the twice-born, who abstain from liquor and meat, and who are constantly engaged in their own duties.
If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity, how should one prescribe the expiation for them in each respective caste? (II,1, p. 417) // Par_11.16 //
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs through eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī;
for a Vaiśya, it is through five thousand, and for a Kṣatriya, through three thousand.
When one eats the food of a Brāhmaṇa, one should cause two thousand [cows] to be given;
or else, one is purified by the Vāmadevya Sāman alone.
"Manu has declared that dry food, cow's milk, and oily substances brought from the house of a Śūdra, once cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, are fit to be eaten. (II.189, p. 427) // Par_11.19 //
If a Brahmin eats in the house of a Śūdra during times of distress,
he may be purified by mental remorse or by reciting the Drupadā verse one hundred times.

A slave, a butcher, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who shares half his earnings—these among the Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (II,1, p. 429) // Par_11.21 //
One born of a Śūdra maiden, if consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa, becomes a Dāsa through that consecration; but if not consecrated, he is a Nāpita.
But the son who is born from a Śūdra woman by a Kṣatriya is to be known as a Gopāla; he is to be fed by Brahmins, without a doubt. (Parāśara 11.23)
One born from a Vaiśya maiden but consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa is to be known as an Ārdhika; he may be eaten by Brāhmaṇas without any doubt.
If one unintentionally consumes water, curd, ghee, or milk that has been placed in a vessel used for forbidden foods, what should the expiation be? (II,1, p. 432) // Par_11.25 //
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who approaches [for instruction],
the expiation for one of the twice-born classes is by means of the Brahmakūrca fast.
For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts.
The *brahmakūrca* rite, even for a single day and night, would purify even a dog-eater.

Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—this is designated as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), which is purifying and a cleanser of sins. (II,1, p. 433) // Par_11.28 //
Cow’s urine from a black cow, cow dung from a white one,
milk from a copper-colored cow, and curd from a red cow are to be taken.
One should take the ghee from a tawny cow, or indeed all [products] from a tawny cow;
one should provide one *pala* of urine and half the size of a thumb of cow dung. (II,1, p. 434) // Par_11.30 //
One should provide seven palas of milk, three palas of curd are prescribed,
one pala of ghee should be given, and one pala of kuśa-water.
Taking cow’s urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam" (II,1, p. 435).

With the mantra "Thou art luster, thou art semen," he should place clarified butter; with "Thee for the God," water from *kuśa* grass; and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) purified by the *ṛc*, he should set them down in the vicinity of the fire.
Having stirred [the water] with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should recite over it the mantra "mā nas toke.
Then, [one should take] seven blades of *darbha* grass that are not cut at the tips and are as bright as a parrot. (II,1, p. 436) // Par_11.34 //

Having drawn these out, one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the rule, reciting the verses beginning with *irāvatī*, *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, *mā naḥ stokāḥ*, and *śaṃvatī*. (II,1, p. 437) // Par_11.35 //

The twice-born should offer oblations with these very [mantras] and drink the remains of the offering after stirring it with the *praṇava* alone, and likewise kindling the fire with the *praṇava*. (II,1, p. 438) // Par_11.36 //
Having drawn it up with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink it with the *praṇava* as well;
for whatever sin resides within the bones of embodied beings in their bodies, [it is removed by this].
The Brahmakūrca burns everything away like a blazing fire consumes fuel;
it is a purifier in the three worlds, presided over by the deities. (II,1, p. 439) // Par_11.38 //
Varuṇa resides in cow urine, and the bearer of oblations (Agni) in cow dung;
Vāyu is declared to be in curd, Soma in milk, and Ravi in ghee.

One should know that water fallen from the mouth into a vessel while one is drinking is unfit for consumption; having drunk it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (II,1, p. 440) // Par_11.40 //
And having seen a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
or having seen bones, skin, and so forth fallen there, or having drunk impure water, a twice-born man [must perform penance].
A human corpse, a crow, a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a gavaya, a supratīka, a peacock, and likewise a rhinoceros; ||| Par_11.42 ||
If one sinks into a well containing the skin of a tiger, a bear, or a lion, or if one has drunk the water of a contaminated pond, [one must undergo purification]. (II,1, p. 441) Par_11.43.
By this sequence, in its entirety, expiation shall be performed by a man;
a Brahmin is purified in three nights, but a Kṣatriya in two days.

But a Vaiśya is purified in one day, and a Śūdra by eating only at night, if he has abstained from another's cooked food and has ceased delighting in another's cooked food. (II,1, p. 446) Parāśara 11.45.
Having eaten the food of an *apacasa*, a twice-born man should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
as for the gift given by an *apacasa*, how can there be any fruit for the giver? (Parāśara 11.46)
Both the giver and the recipient go to hell; having taken the fire and established it, one should not fail to perform the five sacrifices. (II,1, p. 447) // Par_11.47 //
He who has desisted from cooking for others is proclaimed by the sages;
having himself performed the five sacrifices, he subsists on the food of others.
That brahmin who, having constantly risen at dawn, is devoted to the food cooked by others and gives gifts while shunning his own domestic duties, [is a householder in name only].
The sages who know the true nature of dharma have proclaimed that the lower castes are those born from the feet;
for in each successive age, there are specific duties and specific twice-born classes corresponding to them. (II,1, p. 451) // Par_11.50 //
One must not revile them, for those twice-born ones are the very embodiment of the age;
having uttered the sound "hum" to a Brāhmaṇa, or the word "thou" to one who is superior, [one incurs great sin].

Having bathed and spent the remainder of the day standing, he should propitiate [the teacher] by offering salutations, even if he has struck him with a blade of grass or bound him around the neck with a cloth. (Parāśara 11.52)

Even after winning by means of a dispute, one should propitiate him by prostrating; but if one has threatened him, [the penance lasts] for a day and night, and if one has struck him, for three nights. (II,1, p. 455) Par_11.53.
Atikṛcchra is performed when there is blood [in the stool], while kṛcchra is for internal bleeding;
one who eats a handful of food for nine days shall perform the atikṛcchra penance. (II,1, p. 459) // Par_11.54 //
One should fast for three nights; this is called the *atikṛcchra* penance, which is prescribed when a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred. (II,1, p. 460) Par_11.55.
The Gāyatrī, when practiced ten thousand times, is the supreme purification.
If one sees a bad dream, or if one has vomited, undergone a shaving, engaged in sexual intercourse, or been exposed to the smoke from a funeral pyre, bathing alone is prescribed. (II,2,p.1) Par_12.1.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite again. (II,2, p. 5) Parāśara 12.2.
The deerskin, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are set aside for the twice-born upon the performance of the purificatory rite of initiation.
One who has consumed feces or urine shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for purification;
having bathed and partaken of the five products of the cow, he shall become pure. (II,2,p.6) // Par_12.4 //

And for those who have fallen back from their caste through acts such as jumping into water or fire, or through renunciation and fasting unto death—how is purification ordained for them? (II,2, p. 7) // Par_12.5 //
By performing two *prājāpatya* penances, by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
and by the gift of a bull as the eleventh among ten cows, those three castes are purified.
I shall declare the penance for a Brāhmaṇa: having gone to a forest or to a crossroads and shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances.
Svāyambhuva has declared that one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee for purification;
by that, one is released from that sin and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
The wise have proclaimed five meritorious baths:
those pertaining to Agni, Varuṇa, Brahmā, Vāyu, and the divine. (II,2, p. 13) // Par_12.9 //

The fire-related bath is performed with ashes; the water-related bath is by immersion; the Vedic bath is performed with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the wind-related bath is traditionally said to be the dust raised by cows.
But that which occurs during a shower of rain is called a divine bath;
having bathed there, a person becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā. (Parāśara 12.11)
When a twice-born man goes to bathe, all the gods together with the hosts of ancestors follow him in the form of wind, afflicted by thirst and seeking water. (II,2, p. 17) // Par_12.12 //
They return disappointed once the wringing out of the garment has been performed;
therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having first performed the libation for the ancestors.
Whoever, having applied [sesame] to the pores of the skin, should satisfy the ancestors with sesame seeds, by him the ancestors are satisfied with blood and with filth. (II,2,p.18) Par_12.14.
He who shakes his hair after bathing, he who discards impurity,
or he who sips water even while standing in the water— such a person is excluded from the rites of the ancestors and the gods.

Having covered one's head or neck, or even with the lower garment or the topknot hanging loose, one becomes impure even after sipping water if the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is absent. (II,2, p. 19) // Par_12.16 //

One standing on land should not perform ritual sipping (ācamana) while in water, nor one standing outside should do so while in water; having touched both [the water and the ground], and having performed ācamana, one becomes pure in both respects.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road, and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water should sip water again. (II,2, p. 20) [Par_12.18]
Upon sneezing, spitting, or having food remnants on the teeth, as well as upon speaking untruths or conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear.
"Manu has declared that the sacred sites beginning with Prabhāsa and the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā reside within the right ear of a Brahmin. (II.2, p. 20; not in BI) // Par_12.20 //
Fire, water, and the Vedas, as well as the moon, the sun, and the wind—
all these indeed abide in the right ear of the Brahmin.
Bathing during the day is praised when purified by the rays of the sun;
bathing at night is not recommended, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [during an eclipse]. (II,2, p. 21) // Par_12.22(21) //
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and burnt offerings should be performed during the appearance of Rāhu;
otherwise, the night is impure, and therefore one should avoid it.
The Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—indeed, all the deities—are dissolved into the Soma; therefore, a gift should be given at its extraction. (II,2, p. 22) Par_12.24(23)

At a sacrifice for the common folk, at a wedding, at the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign, and likewise during an eclipse, giving is indeed prescribed for the night; it is not ordained for any other occasion.
At the birth of a son, at a sacrifice, during a funeral rite, and upon the sight of Rāhu [an eclipse], giving gifts at night is praised; it is not so at other times.
The "great night" (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle watches;
during the first and last watches, one should perform the bath as one does during the day.
A sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, and a seller of Soma—a Brāhmaṇa who has touched these must enter the water with his clothes on. (II,2, p. 24) // Par_12.28(27) //
Before the collection of the bones, one should perform a bath after weeping;
for within the ten-day period of a Brahmin’s death, there is bathing, but after that, it is merely sipping water (ācamana).
When the sun is seized by Rāhu, all water is equal to the Gaṅgā; the same is declared regarding the eclipse of the moon, for rites such as bathing and giving gifts. (II,2, p. 25) // Par_12.30(29) //
A bath purified by *kuśa* grass, a twice-born man who sips water with *kuśa*, and water drawn up with *kuśa*—each of these is equal to drinking the Soma juice. (II,2, p. 26) // Par_12.31(30) //
Those who have fallen away from the fire-ritual, those who have abandoned the twilight devotions,
and those who do not study the Veda— all these are declared to be *vṛṣalas*.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who is afraid of a Śūdra, especially if he is unable to study the whole, should at least study a single portion. (II,2, p. 27) // Par_12.33(32) //
Even for one who studies constantly, recites prayers, or offers oblations, if he is nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, no upward path exists.

The food of a Śūdra, association with a Śūdra, sitting together on the same seat as a Śūdra, and receiving knowledge from a Śūdra—these will cause even one who is blazing [with spiritual power] to fall. (II,2, p. 28) // Par_12.35(34) //

That twice-born man who constantly has food cooked by a Śūdra woman, and whose housewife is a Śūdra woman, is excluded from the rites for the ancestors and the gods, and he goes to the Raurava hell. (II,2, p. 29) // Par_12.36(35) //
With a body nourished by the impurity of death and birth, and subsisting on the food of a Śūdra,
I do not know what various wombs such a twice-born man will enter.
"For twelve births he shall be a vulture, for ten births a pig, and for seven births he shall be in the womb of a dog; thus Manu has declared. (II,2, p. 30) // Par_12.38(37) //
But that Brahmin who, for the sake of a fee, should offer the oblation for a Śūdra,
becomes a Śūdra, while the Śūdra becomes a Brahmin.
Having undertaken the vow of silence, a twice-born man should not speak while seated;
for if one who is eating should speak, he should avoid that food. (II,2, p. 31) // Par_12.40(39) //
If a Brahmin drinks water from that same vessel while only half of his meal remains uneaten,
he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and brings harm upon himself.
But he who sets down his vessel first while the Brahmins are still eating is a fool and a most sinful man; indeed, he is called a slayer of a Brahmin. (II,2, p. 32) Par_12.42(41)
If the twice-born perform the *svasti* blessing while the vessels remain [empty],
the gods do not attain satisfaction, and likewise the ancestors depart disappointed.
One should never eat without having bathed, nor without having muttered prayers, nor without having offered oblations to the fire;
likewise, one should not eat from the back of a leaf, nor at night without a lamp.

But a householder, endowed with compassion, should reflect only upon dharma; being of sound intellect and walking the path of justice, he should do so for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those whom he must support. (II,2, p. 33) Par_12.45(44)
One must indeed protect oneself with wealth acquired through righteous means;
however, he who lives by unrighteous means is excluded from all ritual acts.

The builder of a fire-altar, a tawny cow, one who has completed a sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify by the mere sight of them; therefore, one should look upon them constantly. (II,2, p. 34) // Par_12.47(46) //

One should keep these things in the house: the fire-drill wood, a black cat, sandalwood, a fine jewel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, a black antelope skin, and a goat. (II,2, p. 35) // Par_12.48(47) //
A field where one hundred cows with a single bull can stand unconfined is proclaimed to be ten times that size as a *gocarma*.

A mortal who has committed the murder of a Brahmin or other sins born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, is liberated from all those evils by the gift of a *gocarma* (a cow-hide). (II,2, p. 36) Par_12.50(49)
Whatever gift is given to a householder who is poor, and especially to one learned in the Vedas, that gift brings about auspicious results. (II,2, p. 37) // Par_12.51(50) //
One who seizes land is not purified by the construction of ponds, wells, and tanks, nor by hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, nor even by the gift of ten million cows.

The sage Uśanas declared that for a woman with menstrual flow, bathing alone is required before eighteen days; beyond that, she must observe a three-night period of impurity. (II,2, p. 38) // Par_12.53(52) //

One *yuga*, two *yugas*, three *yugas*, and four *yugas* [are the periods of impurity] for a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and one who has fallen from his caste, respectively.
Then, by the mere presence [of the impurity], one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
having bathed, one should look at the sun if one has touched it through ignorance. (II,2, p. 39) // Par_12.55(54) //
If a Brahmin, though possessing hands, drinks water from his mouth due to weakness in knowledge,
he will certainly be born in the womb of a dog.
If a man, in anger, declares his wife to be unapproachable, yet later desires her again, he must have it proclaimed in the midst of Brahmins. (II,2, p. 40) // Par_12.57(56) //
One who is exhausted, angry, blinded by darkness, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear,
having failed to perform a meritorious gift, must observe a three-day penance.
One should perform ablutions at the confluence of great rivers three times a day;
and upon completing the vow, one should give a cow as a gift and feed ten Brahmins.
Having eaten the food of a Brahmin who is of bad conduct and who practices forbidden acts, a twice-born man should fast for one day. (II,2, p. 45) // Par_12.60(59) //
By eating the food of a brahmin who is of virtuous conduct and likewise a knower of the Vedānta,
a man is freed from sin within the interval of a day and night.

One who eats food left over from above, food left over from below, food left over in the intermediate space, or likewise during the menstrual period, as well as one who attends a death-impurity, should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (II,2, p. 46) Par_12.62(61)
O Goddess, one should perform ten thousand *kṛcchra* penances and two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
as well as bathe twelve times at a sacred ford (*puṇyatīrtha*) with the head unwetted.
A pilgrimage of two yojanas is prescribed as the equivalent of one *kṛcchra* penance;
likewise, a householder who intentionally causes the emission of semen onto the ground [must perform the same]. (II,2, p. 48) Par_12.64(63)

One who is endowed with the fourfold knowledge should, according to the rule, recite the mantra of the Goddess a thousand times along with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of one who has killed a Brahmin. (II,2, p. 50) Par_12.65(64)
One should prescribe going to the bridge over the ocean as the expiation;
on the path of the bridge-construction, one should practice begging for alms from the four castes.
Avoiding those engaged in forbidden acts, and deprived of both umbrella and shoes, [he should say]:
"I am indeed one of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins. (II,2, p. 51) // Par_12.67(66) //
I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms, a slayer of Brahmins;
I shall dwell among herds of cattle, or in villages, or in cities.
Having gone to these—penance groves, sacred fords, rivers, or springs—and having traveled to the ocean, he shall proclaim his sin. (II,2, p. 52) Par_12.69(68)
Ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long,
it was constructed by Nala under the command of Rāmacandra.
Having seen the Setu of the ocean, one casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having seen the Setu, one whose soul is purified may plunge into the sea.
Or the king, the lord of the earth, should perform the horse sacrifice;
once he has returned home, he approaches it for the purpose of dwelling.
Together with his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for the Brahmins and give one hundred cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those who are proficient in the four Vedas.

Through the grace of the Brahmins, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated; having killed a woman engaged in a Soma sacrifice, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin. (II,2, p. 76) // Par_12.74(73) //
A twice-born man who drinks liquor should go to a river that flows to the ocean;
then, having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, he should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas. (II,2, p. 77) // Par_12.75(74) //
And one should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee to Brahmins;
having drunk liquor even once, one should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire. (II,2, p. 80) // Par_12.76(75) //
Having himself stolen gold from a Brāhmaṇa, he must then purify himself both in this world and in the next. (II,2, p. 84) [Par_12.77(76)]
Taking a pestle, he should go into the presence of the king for execution;
then he attains purification, and he is indeed released by the king.
But that which is done intentionally deserves a different punishment from death;
[this applies to] sitting together, sleeping together, traveling together, conversing together, and eating together. (II,2, p. 90) // Par_12.79(78) //
For sins indeed pass on like a drop of oil upon water; [the penances for this include] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal fast, and the Tulāpuruṣa. (II,2, p. 91) Par_12.80(79)
Following after cows also destroys all sins.
This is the Pārāśara Śāstra, a compendium of the Dharmaśāstra consisting of five hundred and ninety-two verses. (II,2, p. 287; BI: 534)
Just as the duties of Vedic study [are observed], so too must this Dharmaśāstra be studied with diligence and constancy by one who desires to go to heaven. (II,2, p. 288) Par_12.[82](81)
